systems.name: Aquaponics
systems.what: Fish and plants share the same water. Fish waste feeds tiny germs. The germs turn it into food for plants. The plants clean the water for the fish.

systems.name: Hydroponics
systems.what: Plants grow with their roots in water mixed with plant food. There is no soil and no fish. An air pump keeps the water full of air.

systems.name: Aeroponics
systems.what: Roots hang in the air in a dark box. A pump sprays them with a fine mist of plant food. If the mist stops, the plants wilt fast.

fish.name: Tilapia
fish.grow: Grows to about 1⅓ lb in 6 to 8 months. Easy for beginners. Can live with low air in the water, but grows slower.
fish.note: Needs warm water all year, so most people use a heater. Growth slows below 70°F. It dies below about 50°F.
fish.law: Rules vary by state. In Illinois you need an aquaculture permit plus a letter that lets you keep tilapia. You may never let them go in Illinois waters. Check your state before you buy.

fish.name: Channel catfish
fish.grow: Grows to about 1 lb in 9 to 10 months. Tough fish. Can take lower air in the water than most.
fish.note: Feed until they stop eating, then take out what is left.
fish.law: Native to many states. In Illinois, raising any fish to eat or sell needs an aquaculture permit. Check your state.

fish.name: Bluegill
fish.grow: Small fish. Reaches about 2 oz in 10 to 12 months. Good for small home systems.
fish.note: Grows slowly, so you can stock more of them at the start.
fish.law: Native in much of the U.S. In Illinois, raising fish to eat or sell needs an aquaculture permit. Check your state.

fish.name: Largemouth bass
fish.grow: Grows to about 1⅓ lb in 14 to 16 months. Needs high-protein food.
fish.note: Young fish may only be sold in some seasons.
fish.law: In Illinois, raising fish to eat or sell needs an aquaculture permit. Check your state.

fish.name: Rainbow trout
fish.grow: Grows to about 2 lb in 14 to 16 months. Needs very clean water with lots of air.
fish.note: A cold-water fish. Pair it with cool-season crops like lettuce and kale.
fish.law: In Illinois, raising fish to eat or sell needs an aquaculture permit. Check your state.

fish.name: Koi
fish.grow: A pet fish, not grown to eat. It needs less protein in its food than food fish.
fish.note: Good if you want the plants more than the fish.
fish.sell: To sell live fish in Illinois, you need a fish dealer license from the state. We could not check a usual sale size. Ask local buyers and check your state.
fish.law: Pet fish still count as fish. Check your state rules before you buy.

fish.name: Goldfish
fish.grow: A pet fish, not grown to eat. Cheap and tough.
fish.note: Often used as the first fish while a new system starts up.
fish.sell: To sell live fish in Illinois, you need a fish dealer license from the state. We could not check a usual sale size. Ask local buyers and check your state.
fish.law: Pet fish still count as fish. Check your state rules before you buy.

water.name: pH
water.how: Test before you feed the fish.
water.low: Too low: add limestone gravel or crushed shells. They raise pH slowly and safely.
water.high: Too high: wait, since fish waste slowly lowers it. Do not change it more than 0.2 a day.

water.name: pH
water.low: Out of range: plants cannot take up all their food. Fix it slowly with pH up or pH down made for hydroponics.

water.name: Water temperature
water.good: Fits your fish (see the fish list)
water.how: Look at a tank thermometer each day.
water.low: Too cold: wrap the tank and use a tank heater. Feed less.
water.high: Too hot (over 91°F): shade the tank. Fish stop eating when it is too hot.

water.name: Root water temperature
water.low: Warm water holds less air and helps root rot grow. Shade or cool the tank.

water.name: Air in the water (oxygen)
water.good: 5 ppm or more (6 or more is better)
water.how: Test often in a new system. Once it runs well, test less.
water.low: Too low: add or clean air stones. Feed less. Warm water holds less air.

water.name: Ammonia
water.how: Test daily for the first 2 weeks of a new system, then weekly.
water.low: Over 1 ppm: change 1/3 to 1/2 of the water. Stop feeding for a while. Take out old food and dead fish.

water.name: Nitrite
water.low: Over 1 ppm: change part of the water and stop feeding. Check that pH and heat are right for the germs.

water.name: Nitrate
water.how: This is plant food. Some is good.
water.low: Over 120 ppm for a week: swap some water. Use the old water on garden plants.

water.name: EC (plant food strength)
water.good: What your plant food label says
water.how: Use a meter. Your plain water should read under 1 before you add food.
water.low: Too low: add plant food. Too high: add plain water. Mix it well.

water.name: Top off the water
water.good: Keep the tank at the fill line
water.how: Add water lost to heat and plants.
water.low: For fish, let tap water sit a few days with air bubbling first, or use a dechlorinator.

problems.name: Settling tank clogs or spills over
problems.signs: Water spills over the top. Brown waste flows on to the filter and beds. Pipes run slow.
problems.fix: Drain the waste out of the bottom right away. Do it each day from now on. Feed a bit less for a few days. Clear the pipes.

problems.name: Old waste going bad
problems.signs: Thick dark sludge sits in a tank or bed. Ammonia goes up. Fish gasp at the top.
problems.fix: Waste that sits uses up the air and makes ammonia. Drain it out. Add air. Test ammonia. Clean waste out more often.

problems.name: Ich (white spot)
problems.signs: Small white dots on the skin and fins. Fish rub on things or stop eating.
problems.fix: Ask a fish vet or your extension office before you treat. Many fish meds can hurt plants and the good germs.
problems.quarantine: Keep new fish in their own tank for 30 days before they join the system. Do not share nets or hoses.

problems.name: Fin rot and sores
problems.signs: Ragged fins, red spots or open sores. Often starts after rough handling.
problems.fix: Fix the water first. Handle fish less. Ask a fish health expert if fish keep dying.
problems.quarantine: Move sick fish to a separate tank if you can.

problems.name: Cotton fuzz (water mold)
problems.signs: White or brown cotton-like patches on hurt skin.
problems.fix: It grows on fish that are already hurt or sick. Find and fix the first problem.

problems.name: Stressed fish
problems.signs: Gasping at the top, hiding, not eating, or acting slow.
problems.fix: Test the water right away. Low air, ammonia or nitrite are the most common causes. Add air and change some water.

problems.name: Root rot (Pythium)
problems.signs: Roots turn soft and brown instead of white. Plants wilt even in water.
problems.fix: Throw out sick plants right away. Add more air. Keep root water 68 to 72°F. Clean and sanitize before the next crop.
problems.quarantine: Check new plants before they go in.

problems.name: Green water (algae)
problems.signs: Water or tank walls turn green. Air in the water drops.
problems.fix: Block light from the water with covers or shade cloth. Scoop out thick algae.

problems.name: Slime on roots and pipes
problems.signs: Slick film on roots, pipes or the tank.
problems.fix: Clean off old plant bits. Sanitize the parts between crops.

problems.name: Clogged misters
problems.signs: Weak or uneven spray. Dry roots in one spot. Plants wilt.
problems.fix: Clean or swap the nozzle now. Use a fine filter in the line. Hard water can leave scale.

problems.name: Pump or power stops
problems.signs: No flow, no bubbles or no mist.
problems.fix: Fix it fast. Aeroponic roots dry out in minutes. A backup pump or battery helps. Fish need air too.

Check that the air pump runs.
Test pH and EC.
Top off the water.
Check the root water temperature.
Look at roots. They should be white.
Look for green water or slime. Cover any light leaks.
Check that air stones still bubble well.
Pull out sick plants.

Scrub off roots and plant bits first.

safety.text: Keep soap, bleach and chlorine out of a fish system. They hurt the fish and the good germs. Clean fish tanks with plain water and a brush.
For hydro and aero parts with no fish, scrub off dirt first. Then use a cleaner made for hydroponics, or a 1 to 10 bleach mix. Follow the label and rinse well.
Keep new fish apart for 30 days. Give that tank its own net.

plants.name: Leafy greens
plants.note: The easiest crops. They grow fast and need little food.

plants.name: Herbs
plants.note: Grow well in all three. Basil likes warm water.

plants.name: Fruiting crops
plants.note: Need more plant food and support. Best with lots of fish or in buckets of grow stones.

plants.name: Cool-season crops
plants.note: Pair with cold-water fish like trout.

plants.name: Root crops
plants.note: Our sources do not list these for water systems. Grow them in soil instead.

parts.name: Fish tank
parts.job: The fish live here. Their waste goes out with the water to the next tank.
parts.wrong: Waste builds up on the bottom if the water does not flow out well.
parts.clean: Take out food the fish leave each day. Remove dead fish right away.

parts.name: Settling tank (clarifier or swirl tank)
parts.job: Water slows down here, so solid waste sinks. A swirl tank spins the water to push waste down. Clear water leaves from the top.
parts.size: Our sources size it by how fast water flows through. It is often about 15 to 20 gallons for every 100 gallons of fish tank.
parts.wrong: If you do not drain it, waste spills on to the filter and beds. It can clog pipes and rot.
parts.clean: Drain or siphon the waste from the bottom each day. In some states you can put it on a garden. Check your state rules first.

parts.name: Filter tank (screen and biofilter)
parts.job: A screen or pad catches small bits. Then lots of tiny surfaces give good germs a home. The germs turn ammonia into plant food.
parts.size: Make it about 15 to 20 gallons for every 100 gallons of fish tank. Keep air bubbling in it.
parts.wrong: Without air the germs stop working, and ammonia goes up. Old waste here uses up the air.
parts.clean: Rinse the screen in tank water, not tap water. Stir the filter bits now and then. Never scrub them clean or let them dry.

parts.name: Grow beds
parts.job: Plants take up the plant food. This cleans the water for the fish.
parts.wrong: Roots can clog pipes and drains. Waste on roots hurts the plants.
parts.clean: Pull roots out of pipes each week. Wash rafts in water, but do not let them dry out.

parts.name: Sump tank
parts.job: This is the lowest tank. Water drains down into it from the beds.
parts.wrong: If the water gets low, the pump can run dry.
parts.clean: Top it off with water that has no chlorine. Look for leaks.

parts.name: Pump back to the fish
parts.job: A pump at the bottom of the sump sends water back up to the fish tank. Then the loop starts again.
parts.size: Use wide pipes so they do not clog.
parts.wrong: If the pump stops, fish lose air and the beds dry out.
parts.clean: Check each day that it runs and is not blocked.
